n: Paul is appalled that members were suing one another in pagan courts instead of settling disputes within the Church.

f.g: Here, unbelieving judges outside the Church.

n: The saints will one day help judge the world. Surely they can handle small disputes among themselves!

f.w: the saints shall judge the world

n: They will even judge angels — likely fallen angels. How much more can they handle everyday matters?
So if they have ordinary disputes, why hand them to people the Church doesn’t esteem? Many read this as a question rather than a command.

f.g: Those of no standing in the Church — likely the outside judges.

n: Paul says this to shame them: is there really no one wise enough in the congregation to settle a disagreement between members?
Instead, brother sues brother — in front of unbelievers, damaging the Church’s witness.
Having lawsuits at all is already a defeat. Why not rather accept a wrong or a loss than fight your brother in court?
Worse, some of them were the ones doing wrong and cheating their own brothers and sisters in the faith.
Paul reminds them that the unrighteous won’t inherit God’s kingdom, then lists sins that exclude people, including sexual sins and idolatry.

f.w: effeminate, nor abusers of themselves with mankind
f.g: Greek terms generally understood to refer to men taking part in homosexual acts.

n: The list continues: thieves, the greedy, drunkards, verbal abusers, and swindlers will not inherit God’s kingdom unless they repent.

f.g: Those who insult and abuse with words.

f.w: shall inherit the kingdom of God

n: Some of them used to live that way — but Christ changed them. They were washed in baptism, made holy, and declared right with God through Christ and the Spirit. Change is possible.

f.g: Declared righteous, put right with God.

n: Paul quotes a Corinthian slogan, “All things are lawful,” and qualifies it: not everything is helpful, and he won’t be enslaved by anything. JST: “All these things are not lawful unto me.”

f.w: brought under the power of any
f.g: Mastered or enslaved by any habit.

n: Some argued that bodily appetites, like eating, are merely natural. Paul answers that the body isn’t designed for sexual immorality — it is for the Lord, and the Lord cares for the body.

f.g: Food for the stomach — probably another Corinthian slogan.

n: The body matters eternally: God raised Jesus’ body, and He will raise ours by the same power.
Our bodies are members of Christ’s body. How could we join Christ’s members to a prostitute? Absolutely not!

f.g: Greek mē genoito — “May it never be!”

n: Sexual union creates a deep bond. Paul quotes Genesis — “two shall be one flesh” — showing that sex is never merely physical.

f.w: two, saith he, shall be one flesh

n: The person united to the Lord becomes one with Him in spirit — a far higher union.
Run from sexual sin. Unlike other sins, it is a sin against one’s own body, which was meant to be sacred.
Each person’s body is a temple where the Holy Ghost dwells. We don’t belong to ourselves.

f.w: your body is the temple of the Holy Ghost

n: Christ paid the price of our redemption with His own blood. So we honor God in how we use our bodies and spirits.
